C0.quote: A voting rule decides on a probability distribution over a set of m alternatives
C0.note: Probabilistic voting rules aggregating rankings; distortion and proportional fairness.

C1.quote: we study the distortion of voting rules, which is a worst-case measure
C1.note: Main results are distortion and proportional fairness bounds (WD). Also a polynomial-time algorithm (Thm 4.9) and a truthfulness-related lower bound (Appendix D, using strategyproofness as a property), plus core and Nash welfare implications. AX and SB are not clearly main; AX is included only loosely for the core/fairness property results.

C2.1.quote: We refer to the collection ⃗σ = (σi)i∈N as a preference profile.

C2.2.quote: Each agent i ∈ N submits a preference ranking over the alternatives
C2.2.note: Strict rankings via bijective rank function.

C2.3.quote: each agent i has a cardinal utility function ui : A → R⩾0 over alternatives

C2.4.quote: We assume that when agents submit ranked preferences, they have more expressive underlying cardinal preferences.
C2.4.note: Separate notation σ and u, with consistency relation.

C3.1.quote: no agent can increase her utility by misreporting her vote
C3.1.note: Strategyproofness (truthful rules) is analyzed in lower bounds (Thm 4.5, D.8) and as an explanation for harmonic rule; main distortion and PF analyses do not model misreporting.

C3.2.note: Non-strategic analyses use rankings consistent with utilities; no statement that voters submit their held attitude truthfully. Consistency is assumed (u▷σ) but this is definitional for the input-utility link; the paper does not state sincere reporting.

C4.1.quote: we say that a utility function ui for agent i is consistent with her preference ranking

C4.2.note: Paper does not use dichotomous preferences as its own model; only cited in references and related work, and uses approval utilities defined as 0/1 utilities.

C5.1.quote: the utilitarian welfare of a distribution over alternatives x ∈ ∆(A) is defined as
C5.1.note: Distortion, social welfare, proportional fairness, core.

C5.2.quote: Note that voting rules have access to the preference profile but not to the utility profile.
C5.2.note: Evaluated on hidden utilities defined separately from the rankings.

VOT.quote_behav: no agent can increase her utility by misreporting her vote
VOT.quote_info: any preference profile ⃗σ , any agent i ∈ N
VOT.note: Voters submit rankings (fixed) in main analyses; in strategyproofness results voters may misreport. Info: strategyproofness is dominant-strategy, so no knowledge assumed; coded loosely as NONE (implicit). Main analyses: voters nonstrategic.

DES.note: Rule is designed by authors but designer's choice not modelled as an agent.

OTH.note: The adversary in the minimax proof is a proof device, not an agent.

C8.1.quote: A voting rule f is called strategyproof (also known as truthful)
C8.1.note: Strategyproofness used for voters in the lower bound analysis. The minimax theorem is used as a proof tool, not as a solution concept for agents.

C8.2.quote: A voting rule f is called strategyproof (also known as truthful)

if you want to be efficient, it pays to also be fair.
Significant challenges lie ahead in paving the path for increased practicability

C9.1.note: Claims about applications and fairness to voters.

C9.2.quote: reports only the induced ranking over alternatives to the voting rule
C9.2.note: Claims about fairness/efficiency for voters need an assumption that voters report rankings consistent with their utilities (sincere reporting); the paper only defines consistency and does not state that voters submit truthfully outside the truthful-rule results.

C10.1.note: No statement of purely procedural reading.
